content: 1. Over a span of 20 years, hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment was randomly allocated globally and regionally, as depicted in Figure 54. This allocation included populations such as people who inject drugs (PWID), individuals with cirrhosis, and those aged 30 years or older. 2. Figure 3 presents scatter plots illustrating the univariable associations between the number of HCV infections averted per randomly allocated treatment over 20 years and three factors: (a) a country’s population growth rate, (b) the prevalence of HCV antibodies among PWID in 2015, and (c) the population-attributable fraction (PAF) of injecting drug use to HCV transmission in a given country. 3. Figure 3a specifically correlates the population growth rate with the number of HCV infections averted, calculated as (1/22) log (2037 population size / 2015 population size). 4. Figure 3b focuses on the prevalence of HCV antibodies among PWID in 2015 and its relationship to the number of infections averted per treatment. 5. Figure 3c examines the PAF of injecting drug use (IDU) to HCV transmission in a country and its association with the number of infections averted. 6. Figure 4 provides scatter plots of univariable associations between the number of HCV infections averted per treatment given to PWID and the same three factors: (a) population growth rate, (b) HCV antibody prevalence among PWID in 2015, and (c) the PAF of IDU to HCV transmission. 7. Figure 4a again uses the formula (1/22) log (2037 population size / 2015 population size) to represent the population growth rate and its association with infections averted. 8. Figure 4b highlights the prevalence of HCV antibodies among PWID in 2015 and its impact on the number of infections averted per treatment. 9. Figure 4c explores the PAF of HCV infections due to injecting drug use and its relationship to the number of infections averted per treatment. 10. The references cited include a comprehensive range of studies and reports on the global epidemiology, prevalence, and treatment of HCV, as well as the impact of antiviral therapies and prevention strategies on HCV transmission and liver-related morbidity. These references span from global modeling studies to systematic reviews and economic evaluations, providing a robust foundation for understanding the burden of HCV and the effectiveness of interventions.
